Awesome result!

• I use Claude Max, $200/month

  • I spent exactly $0 on this whole formalization, because I simply use my existing Claude subscription, and Aristotle API is free for now :fingers_crossed:

In fact, I am now under the impression that with a slightly better harness Claude could do this whole formalization on its own, without Aristotle. But it would have taken much longer, especially because jobs can be submitted to Aristotle in parallel.

Regarding human work, here is all the work I did in this project: https://github.com/Vilin97/aristotle/blob/landau/scripts/human_prompts.txt. I did not write a single line of Lean code myself.

Have you double-checked the statement of the main theorem? From a quick glance, I can say that the formalized version does not correspond to the informal claim. I'm not telling you where, because I think it's more interesting to let you and/or the AI investigate. Don't hesitate to ask here if you can't see the mismatch.

@Sébastien Gouëzel ,

Have you double-checked the statement of the main theorem?

Yes. It's not exactly the same in several ways: the formal version does not use the conservation laws, and thus does not derive the temperature and the constant magnetic field (those follow from the conservation laws, and require defining and analyzing the actual dynamics, not just the steady-state condition, which I suspect might lead to more difficulty and limited added value). There is also the issue of regularity -- my formal version uses smooth ($C^\infty$) functions, while the optimal regularity is only $C^2$. There is also the issue of the tail behavior: I am assuming the solution to be in the Schwarz class but one can directly assume the finiteness of several key integrals, which would be a weaker assumption but harder to use.

I am okay with all of the discrepancies I outlined above, because they do not change the spirit of the argument, it's just more annoying work to show integrability or differentiability. Did you spot any other discrepancies?

Hi Vasily, very exciting work!
Here is another new mathematical theorem that @Jonas Bayer, many undergrad students and I formalized (in Isabelle) before all co-authors signed off on the first pre-print, from last summer: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20909
Seems like Aristotle+Claude can now (almost) do the same job for which we had some 13 student collaborators. The technical report on just the formalization was presented at ITP last year: https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITP.2025.3
PS. I have been calling this kind of parallel proof writing and formalizing an « in-situ formalization » :)

Vasily Ilin said:

Did you spot any other discrepancies?

Yes, absolutely. The statement does not correspond to the description you just gave in your message.

@Sébastien Gouëzel , my only other guess for the discrepancy you spotted is that the formal theorem does not use the Faraday law curl E = 0. It would be needed to derive the equilibrium temperature and magnetic field, but is not needed to derive the main result -- that the equilibrium of the VML system is a global Maxwellian.

If you spotted something else, please do share. To be clear, I am planning to include this theorem in my upcoming paper (crediting Gemini for the proof), so I really appreciate your thoroughness!

I have just seen that your theorems mention ContDiff ℝ ⊤ (f x) (and so on) which means analytic, not C^\infty. I have not checked at all whether the other definitions like torusCurlX do what they say, but I find it a little bit worrisome that AI can overlook such discrepancies -- if there is one in the only line I've checked, how many others are there?

Have you formalized that the function f x v = equilibriumMaxwellian ρ T v satisfies all the assumptions of the theorem? This would be a good sanity check that the definitions capture what they should.

Have you formalized that the function f x v = equilibriumMaxwellian ρ T v satisfies all the assumptions of the theorem?

I did.

But it doesn't help with your observation regarding analyticity. I have a slightly more relaxed version of the theorem that only uses C^3 different ability: link.

Thank you for pointing out the gap though, I will try to resolve it. Most of my interactions with Claude in this project have been of this exact nature: that some definition looks correct at face value but is actually not mathematically correct. I don't know of a good way of resolving these issues in an autonomous way.

I reduced the smoothness assumptions to the optimal C^2: link

CoulombConcreteTheorem42

theorem CoulombConcreteTheorem42
-- === Physical state at steady state ===
(f : Torus3 → (Fin 3 → ℝ) → ℝ)
(E B : Torus3 → Fin 3 → ℝ)
(ν ρ_ion : ℝ)
-- === Physical parameters ===
(hν : 0 < ν) -- (1)
(hρ_ion : 0 < ρ_ion) -- (2)
(hf_pos : ∀ x v, 0 < f x v) -- (3)
-- === Smoothness ===
(hf_smooth_v : ∀ x, ContDiff ℝ 3 (f x)) -- (4)
(hf_smooth_x : ∀ v, ContDiff ℝ 2 (periodicLift (fun x => f x v))) -- (5)
(hB_smooth : ∀ i, ContDiff ℝ 2 (periodicLift (fun x => B x i))) -- (6)
-- === Schwartz-class velocity decay, uniform in x ===
(hSchwartz : UniformSchwartzDecay f) -- (7)
(hLogGrowth : ∃ (C_log : ℝ) (K_log : ℕ), ∀ (x : Torus3) (v : Fin 3 → ℝ),
|Real.log (f x v)| ≤ C_log * (1 + ‖v‖) ^ K_log) -- (8)
-- === Polynomial score bound (independent of hSchwartz + hLogGrowth) ===
-- This is NOT derivable from hSchwartz + hLogGrowth: the ratio |∂f|/f can grow
-- super-polynomially even for Schwartz f with polynomial log growth.
-- Satisfied by Maxwellians and physically reasonable perturbations.
(hGradBound : ∃ (Cg : ℝ) (Kg : ℕ), ∀ (x : Torus3) (v : Fin 3 → ℝ) (i : Fin 3),
|fderiv ℝ (f x) v (Pi.single i 1)| ≤ Cg * (1 + ‖v‖) ^ Kg * f x v) -- (9)
-- === Steady-state Vlasov equation with Coulomb kernel ===
(hVlasov : ∀ x v,
dotProduct v (torusGradX (fun y => f y v) x) +
dotProduct (E x + cross v (B x)) (vGrad (f x) v) =
ν * LandauOperator coulombKernel (f x) v) -- (10)
-- === Steady-state Maxwell equations ===
(hAmpere : ∀ x, torusCurlX B x = fun i => ∫ v, v i * f x v) -- (11)
(hGauss : ∀ x, torusDivX E x = (∫ v, f x v) - ρ_ion) -- (12)
(hDivB : ∀ x, torusDivX B x = 0) -- (13)
:
-- === Conclusion ===
∃ (T_eq : ℝ) (B₀ : Fin 3 → ℝ), 0 < T_eq ∧
(∀ x v, f x v = equilibriumMaxwellian ρ_ion T_eq v) ∧
(∀ x, E x = 0) ∧
(∀ x, B x = B₀)

Was the waste result of Aristotle (I have noticed the proofs it produces are not the most readable) or Claude's proof architecture pass?

I didn't look very closely what code was removed. But it's in the commits (e.g. this removes 500 LOC). Aristotle's proofs are indeed incredibly verbose. Aristotle seems to only care that the proof compiles, and it tends to produce pretty crazy proofs with exact? and other similar artifacts left in. Claude is very good at cleaning these up. The role of Aristotle in my process is essentially a hammer.

In my experience also Claude is very capable of proving theorems

Indeed. I have a feeling that it would be able to complete this formalization without Aristotle's help but it would probably takes a lot longer.

What is the it that you are asking about doing more incrementally? If it's the 3k LOC compression, I don't see a reason to do it incrementally, because there isn't much real content in this process.

I meant the whole project. I read the chart like dead code was accumulated for 7 days and removed at the end, but some incremental clean up where dead code is found and removed closer to every few hours would be faster. For one I think lean reverifies all proofs when lake build is called, so it might speed up things.

Well, I did clean up a lot of dead code throughout. For example, I had the /cleanup command early on and then I made /simplify. But it's hard to be aggressive in the cleanup before the main theorem is fully proven, because what if that helper lemma that isn't used now will be useful in the future? Also, before the main theorem is done, the API is often in flux. I am happy with that part of the process.

There are several other things I would have done differently, but not this one.

What would people consider 'autonomous' versus 'semi-autonomous' , would autonomous be the high bar of 'single overarching prompt' ? Maybe if not one line of Lean code is human written, this is as practically as close to 'autonomous' as you can really get ?

@Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 , I wrote 0 lines of Lean code for this project (and 0 lines in any other progamming language for that matter) but I did write ~200 prompts directing the process. And to write those 200 prompts I watched Clode Code in real time for an average of ~5 hours a day, so maybe 50 hours total. To be fair, 0 of those prompts were about proof strategy, and all were about definitions and assumptions.

For me, "autonomous" would mean that I paste a (mostly correct) theorem and proof in natural language, and in 4 days get a Telegram alert that the agent is done, and when I look at the definitions and assumptions, I can't find obvious flaws like the one @Sébastien Gouëzel immediately spotted.
@Sébastien Gouëzel , fixed the interactive dep graph and docs. In case it goes down again (I hope not!), here is proof:

Steve Yegge has these 8 phases of software developer evolution with AI - https://steve-yegge.medium.com/welcome-to-gas-town-4f25ee16dd04. In my mind using gen AI in some form (phase 1-4) are semi-autonomous, and it becomes fully autonomous 5-8 when one stops to ever looking or caring about any of details of the Lean proofs. It unlocks formalization to the non-Lean initiated which can be exciting for adoption, but currently carries a high risk of misformalization that it doesn't seem appropriate for math (that is today, who knows about in 3 months or further).

Same debates are going on in software circles, and there are already believers of "we don't need to look at the code" and "non-technical people can build software now". It is different there because code can be run, while proofs are not, so one can start to think why bother reading it when I can just see what the code does when run. After all we don't look at machine code, so aren't we just "climbing the abstraction ladded". I don't agree with that argument but that is a different topic for a different forum.

However, there is no such analog of "running the code" in proofs, so if one doesn't do a lean proof review of AI generated code, the only way to make sure misformalization hasn't happened is to ask another LLM, which is not very assuring.

In theory informalization is not hard -- it's a matter of chasing down the exact definitions. So it should be easy to informalize the main theorem and definitions and make sure they are correct. In practice, there is only so far you can expand the dependency graph of types before the context window is saturated, and without expanding the dep graph, the LLM might misunderstand a definition, like it happened with ContDiff in this thread. Notably though, neither can an average Lean programmer; case in point -- despite the hint by Sébastien, I did not find the mistake in the theorem statement.

My point is that it should already be possible to verify the definitions and assumptions without looking at the code, with good enough prompting and probing.

I wrote 0 lines of Lean code for this project (and 0 lines in any other progamming language for that matter) but I did write ~200 prompts directing the process

+1, the mechanics of who pressed the button, shouldn't matter. The degree of involvement with the formalization process should define the level of autonomy given to the agent. The put it in the context of academic research, where you one of those principle investigators that just got the money for the grad student/ AI agent (very direct analogy because someone is pay for the compute), or you where more intimately involved with the process, like attending the daily standup and giving continuous direction and suggestions.

My point is that it should already be possible to verify the definitions and assumptions without looking at the code, with good enough prompting and probing.

Interesting, aren't you worried about garbage-in-garbage-out type of problem. You are using the same lossy LLM tech that produced the problem to audit it.

The lossiness is not inherent to the LLM tech but to the context. With enough (of correct) context everyone is a genius. The question is how to tell which context is valuable. I conjecture that expanding the types of all definitions and structures in the statement of a theorem and adding this info to the context will make the LLM (and human too) significantly less lossy. But ideally, the agent is smart enough to build its own context, like how expert Lean programmers will know exactly where the biggest difficulties and hidden mistakes may be and check that first.
BTW, my personal opinion is that the reason Claude Code is such an incredible product is context management. It's the biggest pain-point of building an agent, and they handle it for you.

Interesting, I am a bit more radical (which I can afford to say by not being an active mathematician) and feel that the human verification process (which we agree is critical) doesn't even need informal proofs. With some training one can easily read at least the lean statement definitions and rough body of the proofs (or ask the AI to refactor to make them more readable, or add comments, etc). Some readability is lost in the lack of beautifully type set Latex, but more is gained in basic IDE technology - command clicks, hover info, proof state, etc.
And most notably, then one extra hoop through the LLM is skipped
